title: Kind and Safe Chat Rules
body:
Kind and safe chat rules are the first online rules a child learns, because chat is where children first meet the wider internet. The rules are simple and positive: be kind in words, keep personal details private, never agree to move a conversation to a hidden app, and tell an adult when a chat feels strange. Rules stated as what to do, rather than only what is forbidden, are rules a child can actually follow in the moment.

Children remember rules they can say back, and the best test of a chat rule is whether a child can explain it to a friend.

The working method is kind-and-safe chat rules for children. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Be kind in words, even when disagreeing in a game or chat
  2. Keep your real name, school, address, and phone number private
  3. Never move a conversation to a hidden app at a stranger's request
  4. Tell a trusted adult at once when a chat feels strange or scary
  5. Treat every chat partner as a stranger until an adult confirms otherwise

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Kind words rule learned; OK :: Personal details kept private; OK :: No hidden-app moves agreed; OK :: Tell-an-adult rule learned; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. These rules suit younger children best and must grow with the child, which later records cover. They do not replace adult supervision for young children, and they do not cover serious harm, which needs immediate adult and, where appropriate, authority involvement. A common mistake is teaching only what is forbidden, which leaves a child with no good action to take when something happens. title: Never Share Personal Details
body:
Never sharing personal details is the rule that protects a child's identity, location, and routine from strangers. Personal details include full name, school name, address, phone number, photos in uniform, and daily schedules, because each detail alone seems small while several together can identify and locate a child. The teaching method is examples: show a child which details a sample post reveals, and let the child find them, so the lesson is discovery rather than lecture.

Children share details innocently, in answers to friendly questions, which is why the rule must be practiced, not merely stated.

The working method is personal-details privacy for children. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Name the details that stay private: name, school, address, phone, schedule
  2. Practice spotting details in sample posts together
  3. Refuse friendly questions that ask for private details, even from kind strangers
  4. Check photos for uniforms, signs, and locations before sharing
  5. Tell an adult when someone keeps asking for private details

It does not cover data collected by services themselves, which the privacy toolkit pair addresses. A common mistake is assuming a detail is safe because it was shared with one person, since online sharing spreads beyond the first reader. title: Photos and Videos: Think Before Sharing
body:
Thinking before sharing a photo or video means pausing to ask three questions: who is in it, what does the background show, and who will see it. A photo's background can show a school sign, a house number, or a sports uniform, and a video's sound can reveal names and places. Teaching children to ask the three questions before posting turns sharing from an impulse into a choice, and asking permission from everyone pictured teaches respect alongside safety.

Photos are the fastest way children share private details, because a picture carries what words would take paragraphs to say.

The working method is photo-and-video sharing review for children. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Ask who is in the photo or video before sharing
  2. Check the background for signs, numbers, and uniforms
  3. Listen for names and places in the video's sound
  4. Ask permission from everyone pictured
  5. Share only with the audience the child and parent agreed

title: Stranger Contact Online
body:
Stranger contact online is the moment a child must know exactly what to do: stop, do not reply with personal details, save the message, and tell a trusted adult. Strangers online may be kind, funny, and interested in the child's games or hobbies, and that friendliness is precisely the method. The rule is not to judge whether a stranger seems nice, but to follow the same steps every time, so judgment is never required in the moment.

Friendliness is free online, which is why it cannot be the test of safety.

The working method is stranger-contact response for children. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Stop replying when a stranger makes contact or asks personal questions
  2. Do not share personal details, photos, or your location
  3. Save the message or take a screenshot with the sender visible
  4. Tell a trusted adult at once and show the saved message
  5. Block the stranger only after saving, so the evidence is kept

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Reply stopped at first personal question; OK :: No personal details shared; OK :: Message saved with sender visible; OK :: Trusted adult told at once; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. This record teaches a defensive response, not investigation: children must never be asked to continue a conversation to gather more information. Where contact is threatening or persistent, adults should involve the service and, where appropriate, authorities promptly. A common mistake is trying to judge whether a stranger seems nice, instead of following the same steps every time. title: Screen-Time Agreements
body:
Screen-time agreements are short written understandings between parents and children about when, where, and how long screens are used. A good agreement covers device-free meals, charging outside bedrooms at night, homework before entertainment, and what happens when the agreement is broken, stated calmly in advance. Agreements work better than sudden bans because they are negotiated, predictable, and applied to adults too, at least in spirit.

Children accept limits they helped write far more readily than limits imposed without warning.

The working method is family screen-time agreements. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Agree device-free times, such as meals and the hour before bed
  2. Agree charging outside bedrooms overnight
  3. Agree homework and chores before entertainment screens
  4. State calmly in advance what happens when the agreement is broken
  5. Review the agreement together each school term

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Device-free times agreed; OK :: Overnight charging place agreed; OK :: Homework-before-entertainment agreed; OK :: Consequences stated calmly in advance; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Screen time is not a single quantity: homework, creative work, and video calls differ from passive scrolling, and this record does not prescribe any particular number of hours. Families should adapt the agreement to their children's ages and needs, with professional guidance where use becomes compulsive. A common mistake is writing an agreement for children only, while adults scroll through every meal themselves. title: Reporting Upsetting Content
body:
Reporting upsetting content teaches a child that seeing something scary, mean, or confusing online is not their fault and not something to hide. The steps are: close the page or app, do not share the content onward, tell a trusted adult, and use the service's report button together. The adult's response matters most: calm, grateful, and without punishment for having seen it, so the child reports the next time too.

A child's willingness to report depends entirely on the first adult response they receive.

The working method is reporting upsetting content for children. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Close the upsetting page or app at once
  2. Do not share the content onward to friends
  3. Tell a trusted adult calmly and show what was seen
  4. Use the service's report button together with the adult
  5. Talk about what was seen in plain words, without blame

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Upsetting page closed at once; OK :: Content not shared onward; OK :: Trusted adult told; OK :: Report button used together; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. This record covers ordinary upsetting content, not illegal or abusive material, which adults must report through the service and the proper authorities and must never ask a child to preserve or handle. It does not replace professional support where a child is distressed. A common mistake is punishing a child for seeing upsetting content, which guarantees it will be hidden next time. title: Gaming Chat and Friend Requests
body:
Gaming chat and friend requests are where many children first meet strangers, because games reward teamwork with people they have never met. The rules are: play with known friends by default, treat in-game friends as strangers until an adult confirms otherwise, never accept gifts or trades that require moving to another app, and mute or report abusive chat without answering back. Voice chat deserves extra care, since a voice reveals age and identity more than text does.

Games make strangers feel like teammates within minutes, which is exactly why their rules must be set before play starts.

The working method is gaming chat and friend-request rules. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Play with known friends by default and confirm new friends with an adult
  2. Treat in-game friends as strangers until confirmed otherwise
  3. Refuse gifts or trades that require moving to another app
  4. Mute abusive chat without answering back
  5. Report abusive players through the game's own tools

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Known-friends default set; OK :: New friends confirmed with an adult; OK :: Cross-app gifts refused; OK :: Abusive chat muted without reply; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Games differ in their chat controls and moderation, so parents should learn the specific game's settings with the child. This record does not cover in-game spending, which a later record addresses, nor the content rating of any particular game. A common mistake is accepting every friend request to avoid seeming rude, since politeness online costs nothing to a stranger. title: Video Platforms and Recommendations
body:
Video platforms and recommendations shape what children watch next, because autoplay and recommendation feeds choose for the viewer. The habits are: choose videos deliberately rather than following autoplay, use the platform's child or restricted settings where offered, recognize that a recommendation is a guess by a system, not a recommendation by a person, and stop watching and tell an adult when a video feels wrong. Watching together, at least sometimes, teaches a child how to choose, not only what to avoid.

Autoplay removes the moment of choice, and choice is the skill children need most on video platforms.

The working method is video platform and recommendation habits. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Choose videos deliberately instead of following autoplay
  2. Turn on the platform's child or restricted settings where offered
  3. Explain that recommendations are system guesses, not personal advice
  4. Stop and tell an adult when a video feels wrong
  5. Watch together sometimes and talk about choices made

This record does not review any particular platform's safety, which parents should check for the services their children actually use. title: Cyberbullying: Stop, Save, Tell
body:
Cyberbullying response follows three words a child can remember under stress: stop, save, tell. Stop means do not reply in anger, since replies fuel the exchange. Save means keep the messages with sender and date visible, because evidence is what adults and services act on. Tell means show a trusted adult at once, and keep telling until someone acts, since the first adult told is not always the one who can help.

A child under attack cannot improvise a good response, which is why the response must be three words long.

The working method is cyberbullying stop-save-tell response. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Stop: do not reply in anger to bullying messages
  2. Save: keep messages with sender and date visible
  3. Tell: show a trusted adult at once
  4. Block the sender after saving, through the service's tools
  5. Keep telling until an adult acts, and record who was told

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: No angry reply sent; OK :: Messages saved with sender and date; OK :: Trusted adult told at once; OK :: Sender blocked after saving; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. This record covers peer bullying response, not bullying by adults or bullying that involves threats, images, or persistent harassment, which need prompt adult, school, and where appropriate authority involvement. title: In-App Purchases and Tricky Offers
body:
In-app purchases and tricky offers target children precisely because children do not yet judge value, pressure, and fine print the way adults do. The defenses are: purchases require an adult's approval, offers that demand speed or secrecy are refused, free items that require personal details are treated as purchases, and every purchase is reviewed together afterwards. A child who understands that free in a game rarely means free has learned the central lesson.

Games are designed to make spending feel like playing, which is why the approval rule must be set before play, not during it.

The working method is purchase and tricky-offer defenses for children. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Require an adult's approval for every purchase, without exception
  2. Refuse offers that demand speed, secrecy, or immediate action
  3. Treat free items that ask for personal details as purchases
  4. Review every purchase together afterwards, calmly
  5. Turn on purchase approval controls on the device and store

title: School Devices and Homework Online
body:
School devices and homework online bring school rules into the home, and the practices are: use the school account only for school work, keep personal accounts off school devices, treat school chat as a classroom where teachers may read it, and tell a teacher or parent when school platforms show something wrong. A school device is borrowed, so its care matters: charged, updated, and returned in the condition it arrived.

A school device is a classroom that fits in a bag, and classroom manners apply wherever it is opened.

The working method is school device and homework practices. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Use the school account only for school work
  2. Keep personal accounts and personal files off school devices

title: Social Media Readiness
body:
Social media readiness is a checklist a family works through before a child opens a first social account, rather than a single age number. The checklist covers: understanding privacy settings, handling stranger contact, recognizing pressure and comparison, knowing how to report and block, and agreeing what the account is for. Readiness is earned by demonstrating the earlier habits in this pair, not by reaching a birthday, and families may reasonably decide a child is not ready yet.

Age opens the door, but readiness decides whether a child can walk through it safely.

The working method is social media readiness checklist. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Demonstrate privacy settings knowledge on a practice account
  2. Demonstrate stranger-contact response without prompting
  3. Discuss pressure, comparison, and the curated nature of feeds
  4. Demonstrate reporting and blocking without help
  5. Agree together what the account is for and its audience

title: Peer Pressure and Dares Online
body:
Peer pressure and dares online are powerful because they arrive from friends, not strangers, and refusal feels like disloyalty. The resistance skills are: a ready refusal phrase that does not invite argument, a private exit from group chats that turn harmful, a trusted adult who can be blamed for the refusal, and the understanding that a dare involving danger, illegality, or humiliation is not a test of friendship. Practicing refusal phrases aloud, before they are needed, is what makes them available under pressure.

Refusal is a skill, not a character trait, and skills are built by practice, not by lectures.

The working method is peer pressure and dare resistance. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Learn a short refusal phrase that needs no argument
  2. Practice refusal phrases aloud before they are needed
  3. Leave group chats that turn harmful, without announcement if needed
  4. Use a trusted adult as the reason for refusal when helpful
  5. Tell an adult when a dare involves danger, humiliation, or illegality

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Refusal phrase learned; OK :: Refusal practiced aloud; OK :: Harmful group chats exited; OK :: Dangerous dares reported to an adult; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. This record teaches refusal for ordinary peer pressure, not intervention in dangerous challenges, which need immediate adult involvement and must never be attempted to prove a point. It does not replace counseling where peer pressure has already caused harm. A common mistake is believing that a dare from a friend is safer than the same dare from a stranger, when the danger is identical. title: When Something Goes Wrong: Family Response Plan
body:
A family response plan for online incidents is written before anything goes wrong, so that a frightened child and a worried parent both know the next step. The plan names: who the child tells first, how evidence is saved, which adult contacts the school or service, and the promise that telling never brings punishment for the telling itself. Families that rehearse the plan once, calmly, discover its gaps while they are still harmless.

A plan rehearsed calmly is followed under stress; a plan invented during a crisis is not a plan at all.

The working method is family response plan for online incidents. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Name who the child tells first, and a second person if the first is unavailable
  2. Agree how evidence is saved before blocking
  3. Agree which adult contacts the school or service
  4. Promise that telling never brings punishment for the telling
  5. Rehearse the plan once calmly and fix the gaps found

Use and limits. A family plan handles ordinary incidents, not serious harm, illegal material, or threats, which need prompt professional and authority involvement and must never wait for a family meeting. title: Teaching Younger Siblings
body:
Teaching younger siblings lets an older child turn their own safety knowledge into leadership, which deepens it. The method is: the older child shows one habit, watches the younger child try it, praises the attempt, and reports difficulties to a parent rather than solving them alone. The parent's role is to confirm the teaching, correct gently where needed, and ensure the older child never becomes the family's only safety authority for a younger child.

Teaching is the best test of understanding, and an older sibling is often the teacher a younger child will actually listen to.

The working method is older children teaching younger siblings. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Show one habit at a time, on the younger child's own device
  2. Watch the younger child try it and praise the attempt
  3. Correct gently and show again, without taking over
  4. Report difficulties to a parent rather than solving them alone
  5. Celebrate when the younger child teaches the habit back

title: Growing Independence: Graduated Freedoms
body:
Growing independence through graduated freedoms means new online freedoms arrive as earlier habits are demonstrated, not all at once. The ladder might run: supervised use, then independent use with checks, then a first account with agreed limits, then wider freedoms with regular reviews. Each step is earned by practice and can be paused without shame if a step proves too much, because a paused freedom is a lesson, not a failure.

Freedom granted gradually is freedom a child has practiced handling, while freedom granted all at once is freedom nobody has practiced at all.

The working method is graduated freedoms by demonstrated practice. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Define the next freedom clearly before granting it
  2. Grant it only after earlier habits are demonstrated
  3. Review the new freedom together after an agreed period
  4. Pause a freedom without shame if it proves too much
  5. Celebrate each step that is handled well
